10099-towards-the-goal:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1917 book, with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt and dedicated to André Chevrillon, true son of France and true friend of England, reports England's effort in the Great War. It follows her earlier England's Effort, tracing the rapid march of events.

Ward visits munition areas, watching enormous and rapid work, and writes of the navy, an aerodrome, and the task of aviators, with Herr Zimmermann and national training among her themes. She writes as a convinced supporter of the Allied cause. Readers get a wartime report from a famous novelist turned observer.
10140-rhetoric-and-poetry-in-the-renaiss:
Donald Lemen Clark, assistant professor of English at Columbia University, published this 1922 study of rhetorical terms in English Renaissance literary criticism. Part first sets out the general theory of rhetoric and of poetry, with an introduction on the distinction between the two arts.

Classical poetic theory follows, through Aristotle and Longinus, the ancient critics Renaissance writers read. Clark writes for students of literature, with care for terms and their history. Readers get a scholarly guide to how Renaissance England talked about poetry, and why its words still matter. His examples come from the critics themselves.
10361-the-creative-process-in-the-indivi:
T. Troward published this metaphysical study in 1915, on how the mind creates its own life. Troward, a writer on New Thought, opens with the old saying that order is heaven's first law. He argues that progress comes not from new laws of nature, but from arranging known things in a better order.

Chapters treat the starting point, self-contemplation of spirit, the divine ideal, the personal factor, race thought, and the divine offering. A Whitman motto frames the book's hope for human grandeur. Readers get a calm, idealist philosophy of creation, aimed at readers seeking spiritual self-command.
10603-with-kelly-to-chitral:
Lieutenant W. G. L. Beynon, staff officer to Colonel Kelly's relief force, wrote this frontier memoir in 1896, as a letter to his mother from Gilgit in October 1895. Beynon warns that his short history holds no heroic deeds, only daily life of British officers and Indian troops on a frontier expedition. Marches, food, jokes, and trials fill the days.

Chapters follow the march, the Shandur Pass, Laspur to Gasht, a reconnaissance from Mastuj, a fight at Nisa Gol, and the goal at Chitral. Snow, rain, hot valleys, and pleasant fields mark the route. Readers get a vivid, soldier's-eye account of a famous relief march on India's northwest frontier.
10985-the-infant-system-for-developing-t:
Samuel Wilderspin, inventor of the infant school system, set out his method in this book, revised in an eighth edition in 1852. Wilderspin had taught more than twenty-five thousand children under six and organised scores of schools across Britain. He argues that children from one to seven should learn through play, objects, and short lessons, not long hours of rote work.

Gallery lessons, Wilderspin insists, should last no more than an hour or two, with mornings for teaching, afternoons for object lessons, spelling, and outdoor moral and physical training. Robbing children of play to show off precocity, he warns, harms health and defeats learning. The book remains a landmark in early childhood education, shaping how infant schools were built and run.
10988-the-devil-s-admiral:
Frederick Ferdinand Moore set this 1913 sea adventure aboard the cargo steamer Kut Sang in the China Sea. The narrator, Trenholm, joins Captain Riggs and his crew for a night and a day of fighting, spying, and piracy. A missionary, a red-headed beggar, a dead boatswain, and a spy called Thirkle drive a plot of gold, thieves, and a battle on the bridge.

Riggs at first refuses to have the story told, fearing he will look beaten, though the narrator insists he was the bravest man aboard. Mouldy biscuit, warm water, and a forecastle mess show the rough side of cargo-boat life. Moore writes a fast yarn of the old China trade, full of fights in the dark and councils of war.
10999-tales-of-bengal:
S. B. Banerjea wrote these seventeen tales of Bengal, edited by Francis Henry Skrine. Stories include the Pride of Kadampur, rival markets, a foul conspiracy, an outrageous swindle, a peacemaker, a Brahman's curse, and a rift in the lute. Village life, joint family estates, markets, and magistrates supply the plots, with morals such as patience and economy stated plainly.

The introduction argues against the idea that East and West can never meet, noting Bengal's fertile, silt-rich soil, its ancient civilisation, and its vulnerability to malaria and invaders. Banerjea writes for English readers, explaining Bengali customs from inside. The tales give a vivid, humane picture of rural Bengal under British rule, told with humour and local knowledge.
11432-the-youth-s-coronal:
Hannah Flagg Gould's 1851 Youth's Coronal, addressed to the youth of her country, aims to entertain and instruct at once. pleasant as spring blossoms in reading and fruitful as ripened fruit in afterlife influence. Gould borrows her title from Proverbs, instruction as an ornament of grace, and promises no moral a good and judicious parent would not wish a child to imbibe. Her coronal is woven of little flowers of poesy, scented and thornless, offered for the giver's sake.

Gould, author of Poems, writes verse and short pieces for young readers in a didactic, affectionate voice. The book belongs to the gift-book tradition for children, where poetry served character formation. Readers of nineteenth-century children's literature will find its preface a clear statement of its method.
11632-woman-man-s-equal:
Thomas Webster's 1873 book, with an introduction by Bishop Simpson, argues for woman as man's equal from nature, history, and the Word of God. Publishers call it a discussion of one of the most important topics of the day, presented in a manner at once attractive and convincing.

Webster sets out abuses suffered by women in heathen nations and brute ages, and says Christianity enlarged woman's area and multiplied her duties. America, he claims, stands ahead of all nations in opportunity. A later passage notes that men who preach female inferiority are often led and duped by frivolous women.
11722-first-lessons-in-geography-or-intr:
James Monteith's First Lessons in Geography, dated 1856, is number one in the National Geographical Series. It serves as an introduction to his Youth's Manual for beginners in schools. Later numbers in the series cover junior, intermediate, and advanced classes, by Monteith and McNally.

Lessons run in question and answer form throughout the book, with the pupil learning states, rivers, and divisions of land by heart. The southern states are counted at ten in one lesson, with Texas named as the largest and Florida as the furthest south. Florida is called a peninsula, and Cuba is named as the island south of it. The book is a school primer meant for recitation aloud.
11754-forty-years-in-south-china-the-lif:
John Gerardus Fagg, missionary of the American Reformed Church at Amoy, wrote Forty Years in South China as a life of Rev. John Van Nest Talmage, published in 1894. An introduction by T. De Witt Talmage says his brother, called the hero of the family, turned down a Brooklyn call with a large salary to go to China.

Chapters run from the ancestral home and a call to China, through the city of the elegant gate, to market towns and country churches. One passage praises babes in Christ whose knowledge of Scripture is remarkable, and recalls W. C. Burns, first English Presbyterian missionary to China in 1847. The book is a missionary biography of steady labour.
12041-the-shadow-of-the-cathedral:
Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's Shadow of the Cathedral, translated from Spanish by Mrs. W. A. Gillespie with a critical introduction by W. D. Howells, appeared in 1919. Its first chapter opens at dawn, as Gabriel Luna arrives in front of the cathedral, though in the narrow street of Toledo it is still night.

Silvery morning light scarcely touches the eaves and roofs, spreading slowly over the old city, while Luna enters the shadow of the great church that will dominate his story. Blasco Ibáñez, a Spanish novelist of passion and politics, uses Toledo's cathedral as both setting and symbol: faith, history, and human desire contending in a single, ancient place.
12896-essays-sthetical:
George H. Calvert's Essays Æsthetical, published in 1875, meditates on beauty, poetry, style, Dante, Sainte-Beuve, Carlyle, national drama, and the usefulness of art. The opening essay calls beauty an immortal theme, born on the same day as the sun, easy in its riches and hard in its demands. Calvert writes as a thoughtful American man of letters.

A passage on style, quoting Buffon, stresses sequence and close dependence of thought and word, detesting a chopped, jerky manner. Composition, Calvert says, begins when separate threads are woven into a continuous whole. The essays suit readers who enjoy nineteenth-century reflection on art and letters.
13248-mckinlay-s-journal-of-exploration-:
John McKinlay's Journal of Exploration in the Interior of Australia records the Burke Relief Expedition, published at Melbourne by Bailliere with three maps. McKinlay, leader of the relief party, writes to the Chief Commissioner of Crown Lands from Depot Camp at Cudye-cudyena in October 1861. His journal runs day by day, with chart and detail.

Entries note horses, bullocks, camels, and sheep all right, save a lame ewe heavy in lamb lost overnight. McKinlay crosses creeks, marks trees MK, names Marchant Creek for William Marchant of Mananarie, and passes quartz reefs and spinifex. The journal is a plain, daily record of search in harsh country, made by a man seeking lost explorers.
13554-aftermath-part-second-of-a-kentuck:
James Lane Allen's Aftermath, part second of A Kentucky Cardinal, was published in 1899. It returns to a Kentucky garden where the narrator works butterbeans, a vegetable of solid merit, while Georgiana watches from her window. She teases him for loving vines, and asks if he expects her to be a vine when they are married.

Congressmen seeking a military asylum for disabled soldiers wander to Lower Blue Lick Springs, Louisville, Frankfort, Maysville, Paris, and Lexington. Georgiana warns that everybody is sensitive in an extraordinary time, while the narrator replies that men must choose liberty for mind and prison for body, or the reverse. Allen writes a Kentucky love story in garden talk and aphorism.
13979-for-the-admiral:
W. J. Marx wrote For the Admiral in 1906, a Huguenot adventure novel set in sixteenth-century France. A perilous ride, a fight by the way, and keeping a ford open the chapters. A traitor to the king, an unknown cavalier, and a commission for the admiral follow. The tragedy of Jarnac and a glorious victory test the heroes.

Marx dedicates the book to his wife, without whose encouragement it would never have been written. A heroine sets aside fear, for the admiral's safety is at stake, and Huguenots gladly sacrifice for their leader. The novel follows Coligny's party through war and faith. It suits young readers of historical adventure. Marx writes with brisk, loyal enthusiasm.
13989-the-duty-of-disobedience-to-the-fu:
Lydia Maria Child addressed this 1860 appeal to the legislators of Massachusetts. Published as Anti-Slavery Tract number nine, it urges disobedience to the Fugitive Slave Act. Child opens with Deuteronomy: thou shalt not deliver an escaped servant to his master. She apologises not for speaking as a woman, citing Scott on truth's right to a tongue.

Child pictures children torn from tender arms by slave traders, and Bibles sealed from people of black, brown, or yellow skin. She argues that unjust law deserves resistance, not obedience. Her prose is earnest, biblical, and political at once. The tract shows women shaping abolitionist argument. It remains a strong statement of higher-law doctrine.
14625-military-instructors-manual:
Captain James P. Cole and Major Oliver Schoonmaker wrote this Military Instructors Manual for the Plattsburg training camps, under Colonel Wolf's supervision, with help from candidates Alcott, Farrar, Elwell, and Prouse. The manual trained officers for the Great War.

It covers rifle grenades, including the Newton Improved with a range of 250 yards and the Hale No. 3, and insists that dummy grenades precede live ones, since carelessness with weapons cannot be tolerated. Drill, throwing, and safety fill the pages. The book is a practical wartime handbook, direct and technical. Plattsburg trained thousands of new officers for France.
14628-the-sweet-and-touching-tale-of-fle:
Mrs. Leighton translated this medieval legend of Fleur and Blanchefleur from the French, with thirty-seven colored illustrations by Eleanor Fortescue Brickdale, published in London in 1922. The tale begins in the year 624.

A heathen king of Spain ravages Christendom, and two children, Fleur and Blanchefleur, grow up together, are parted, and seek each other across ports and courts. A hostess at Nicaea recalls a sighing maiden sold for a great price. The legend is a tender romance of faithful love, retold here in graceful modern English for new readers. Brickdale's illustrations add color to the old tale.
15067-the-cathedral:
J. K. Huysmans's novel, first published in France in 1898 and translated by Clara Bell, follows Durtal, a writer drawn to the cathedral at Chartres. Each morning he crosses a windswept square to enter the vast, dim church, where nuns and bent women hurry through the cold. The building itself becomes the book's true subject.

Durtal studies stone, glass, sculpture, and liturgy, and weighs his own faith against the art around him. Huysmans writes in dense, sensory prose, lingering on scent, light, and detail. Readers who love cathedrals, medieval art, or slow, meditative fiction will find the novel rich, strange, and deeply felt.
15092-the-aldine-vol-5-no-1-january-1872:
Issued in New York in 1872, this art journal mixes essays, poems, and travel notes with fine engraved plates. Its pages range from Alpine scenery and American home life to notes on books, music, and the work of painters. The whole volume was meant to show off both good writing and good printing.

Contributors include well-known names of the day, alongside unsigned editorial pieces on art and taste. Short poems sit beside longer talks on architecture, nature, and foreign lands. Taken together, the number gives a clear sense of what a cultured American reader in the 1870s prized in art, letters, and the wider world.
15180-the-honorable-percival:
Alice Hegan Rice's 1914 novel follows Percival, a blighted being in need of a counter-irritant, through convalescence, counter-currents, and a stranding by the sea. Chapters move from a wind-shelter and a day that never was to a crow's-nest, a gymkhana, and a siren's song. Percival procrastinates, then rises to an occasion.

Rice, known for Mrs. Wiggs, writes with humor about a man adrift who finds purpose, love, and a port at last. Surf boats, wharves, and seaside talk fill the scenes. Readers who enjoy light, character-led romance will find Percival charming, funny, and gently moral.
15352-venereal-diseases-in-new-zealand-1:
This 1922 New Zealand report, from a Board of Health committee chaired by W. H. Triggs, studies venereal diseases and their control. Members include doctors, a hospital board representative, and Lady Luke, with Sir Donald McGavin as medical services director. The report went to both houses of the General Assembly.

Sections cover inquiry scope, ignorance, sex education for the young, syphilis and gonorrhoea, diagnosis, and early, completed treatment. The tone is official, medical, and frank for its day. Public health historians will find the report a revealing record of how a dominion faced a sensitive subject.
15483-rambles-and-recollections-of-an-in:
Major-General Sir W. H. Sleeman wrote these rambles and recollections of India, revised and annotated by Vincent A. Smith for Oxford University Press in 1915. Sleeman dedicates the book to his sister, recalling how letters from home cheered Englishmen in India. Notes moved to chapter ends in this edition, and spelling follows the printed original.

Chapters range widely: fairs on sacred rivers, Hindu religion, the legend of the Nerbudda, a suttee, Hindu marriages, castes, witchcraft, and the peasantry and land settlement. Sleeman writes as an official who traveled, talked, and watched, mixing anecdote with observation. The volume gives a long, detailed view of early nineteenth-century India, valuable for its firsthand scenes even where its judgments belong to its age.
1651-the-mystery-of-orcival:
Émile Gaboriau's detective novel begins on a July morning at Orcival, where poachers find signs of violence near the Seine and a young countess is missing from her home. A local magistrate, a doctor, and the sharp-eyed M. Plantat piece together footprints, a broken window, and a household full of people with reasons to lie.

The investigation turns on money, marriage, and an old scandal, and Gaboriau lets the reader watch the case build clue by clue rather than by sudden confession. As one of the early French crime novels, it shows the police procedural taking shape. Careful inquiry and false leads lead toward a solution that reorders everything the village thought it knew.
1747-the-red-seal:
A New York police court hears a banker named Benjamin Clymer testify about his late housemate Judge Hildebrand and a clerk called John Sylvester. A red seal on a document soon refuses to fit any easy story. A death soon follows, and a red seal on a document becomes the clue that will not fit any easy story.

The novel follows the inquiry through apartments, offices, and society rooms, with Barbara and her circle adding comedy to the suspense. Lincoln writes in the brisk manner of the 1920s detective story. The puzzle turns on character as much as on evidence: who had reason to lie, and who stood to gain from a dead man's papers.
181-the-project-gutenberg-rst-manual:
Project Gutenberg's RST Manual teaches volunteers to build ebooks from plain-text sources. The manual centers on EpubMaker, the project's converter from PG-RST to HTML, EPUB, PDF, and plain text. Opening sections cover installing Python and setup tools on Windows.

Later guidance walks through markup, tables, figures, and contents for a finished ebook. The manual's own structure models the format it teaches, with title pages and lists. Volunteers use it to turn raw texts into readable editions. It documents the workflow behind thousands of Gutenberg books. The manual remains useful for anyone converting plain text into polished ebooks.
1839-other-things-being-equal:
A humming-bird dips to a palm below an open window on a hazy California morning. The novel that follows is a romance of mixed marriage and divided loyalty. What follows, set among San Francisco Jews and Gentiles, is a tale of mixed marriage and divided loyalty. It takes its title from the condition that never quite holds.

A man shorn of his two loves through the same medium that robbed him of his birthright turns to vengeance. The novel follows the cost of that turn. Wolf writes with sympathy for both sides of her divided world. The book is notable as an early American novel to treat Jewish life from within, without apology or caricature.
1929-the-school-for-scandal:
R. B. Sheridan's School for Scandal, a comedy, remains the classic English comedy of manners, built around the Surface brothers: Joseph, the hypocrite, and Charles, the spendthrift with a heart. The scandal school itself is a circle of gossips — Lady Sneerwell, Crabtree, and Sir Benjamin Backbite — who invent reputations for fun.

In one scene, Lady Teazle swears her color is natural, having seen it come and go. Crabtree answers that it goes at night and comes again in the morning, and the exchange shows Sheridan's wit at its sharpest. The play's plot turns on a screen, a portrait, and a test of character. It has held the stage for over two centuries because its jokes about gossip never date.
19745-something-of-men-i-have-known-with:
Adlai E. Stevenson served as Vice President under Grover Cleveland. Something of Men I Have Known gathers his recollections of public life. The contents promise chapters like Cleveland As I Knew Him. Others include A Camp-Meeting Orator and The Sage of the Bar. A piece called The Gentleman from Mississippi recalls Senate figures. The tone is that of an insider telling stories after dinner.

Political memoirs of this kind trade in portraits, not policy. Stevenson had practiced law and politics in Illinois for decades. He knew the men who ran the post-Civil War republic. His sketches preserve their talk, humor, and habits. Historians mine such books for color. Readers get a front-row seat at a vanished Washington.
19961-aboriginal-remains-in-verde-valley:
Cosmos Mindeleff surveyed aboriginal remains in Arizona's Verde Valley. His report appeared in the Bureau of Ethnology's Thirteenth Annual Report. Written history of the region extends back only a few years, he notes. Since the aboriginal inhabitants abandoned it, Apache and Walapai roamed there unhindered. Cliff houses and pueblos stood empty above the river. Mindeleff mapped and described them for science.

The Verde Valley holds some of the Southwest's richest ruins. Mindeleff, brother of Victor, worked the same federal survey tradition. His plans recorded sites before looting thinned them. Montezuma Castle country is his terrain here. The report joins description to careful measurement. It remains a baseline for Verde Valley archaeology.
20120-the-priest-the-woman-and-the-confe:
Father Chiniquy wrote The Priest, the Woman, and the Confessional, a fierce attack on Catholic confession. Chiniquy had been a Catholic priest before he left that church. He then spent years preaching and writing against its teachings. Scripture fills his pages, quoted to back each charge he makes.

One passage cites Ezekiel on sins that fill a land with violence. Chiniquy reads such texts as proof against the confessional itself. The book stirred strong feeling on both sides when it appeared. It remains a stark record of religious conflict in the nineteenth century.
20209-history-of-steam-on-the-erie-canal:
History of Steam on the Erie Canal traces steam power on New York's great waterway. From 1858 to 1862, a first series of steamers proved the idea. Their success sparked wide enthusiasm for steam transport on the canal. That fall, the governor and Canal Board toured by chartered steam-tug.

Public receptions and speeches greeted them at cities along the route. Steam promised faster, cheaper freight than horse-drawn canal boats could give. Yet locks, size, and cost all limited steam's canal future in fact. Readers get a close record of a key shift in American transport.
20307-kate-s-ordeal:
Emma Leslie wrote Kate's Ordeal, a tale for girls of school and sudden change. Kate races to catch her friends before they reach the school gates. She fans herself with her handkerchief and brings great news breathlessly. She is going to London, she tells them with a triumphant glance.

That glance is aimed at Esther Odell, who called her proud and stuck-up. London, to a country schoolgirl, means wonder, risk, and a test of character. Leslie wrote many tales where faith steadies girls in new trials. Young readers get excitement with a clear moral thread running through.
20924-ely-cathedral:
Cardinal de Luxemburg's tomb, built into the north wall, marks one stop in Ely Cathedral. The retro-choir holds Dr. Mill, a Hebrew scholar from Cambridge, who died in 1853. Faint wall paintings with no known tale mark the east wall's close.

Guidebooks in the Bell's Cathedrals set walk readers stone by stone through great churches. Ely's vast nave, lady chapel, and lantern tower star in this volume. Dates, tombs, and carved work unfold in calm, exact order. The book serves walkers in the church and armchair readers alike, keeping Ely's long past in one handy, trusted guide.
20959-mexico-its-ancient-and-modern-civi:
Thanks for photos crowd the front of Mexico, a survey of its ancient and modern civilisation. The Mexican Financial Agency, rail firms, and banks all aided the plates. C. Reginald Enock built his book with help from men on the ground.

Aztec ruins, mines, farms, railways, and politics fill Enock's wide account. He treats Mexico's past glory and its modern push for growth as one tale. British readers then weighed Mexico for trade and travel in its pages. The book stands as a full, dated portrait of the country on the eve of its great revolution.
21097-tom-finch-s-monkey-and-how-he-dine:
John C. Hutcheson gathers five short late Victorian yarns in this volume, opening with a monkey dressed as an officer aboard ship. The pet is presented to a visiting admiral, who invites all the officers to dinner and asks especially for the quiet one. The tale plays the joke out at sea off Callao.

Other pieces explain icebergs and follow a yachting cruise among the Greek islands. There the party saves a Greek's life and meets bandits. A third reports the sea serpent sighted by HMS Daedalus in 1848. A curious cricket match closes the set. Sea humour ties the five together.
21900-the-principles-of-breeding-or-glim:
Better farm animals through science is S. L. Goodale's aim in The Principles of Breeding, published at Boston in 1861. Goodale, secretary of the Maine Board of Agriculture, says farmers lacked a handy book of the principles behind improvement. His subtitle promises glimpses at the physical laws of reproduction in domestic animals. A transcriber's note warns modern readers that neat cattle are cattle of the bovine kind, not tidy dressers.

Goodale writes for working breeders, not scholars, and keeps the book compact. Heredity, selection, and crossing are handled in plain terms for the farm. The volume shows American agriculture reaching for science just before the Civil War. Its ideas, some since refined away, shaped the breeding sheds of its day.
22035-dramatized-rhythm-plays-mother-goo:
John N. Richards published Dramatized Rhythm Plays in 1922 for teachers of young children. The book turns Mother Goose rhymes and old singing games into small plays acted in rhythm. Little Jack Horner, Humpty Dumpty, and Sing a Song of Sixpence all appear. So do See Saw Marjory Daw and Dickory Dickory Dock.

Louise Westwood, who directed music in the Newark public schools, helped with the musical side. Words and tunes came, with permission, from J. Elliott's nursery rhyme settings. The aim was exercise, music, and play in one lesson. Such rhythm work was a proud feature of progressive classrooms in the 1920s.
22040-prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-3-january:
The Prairie Farmer had served farm families from Chicago since 1841. This weekly issue, volume 56 number 3, is dated January 19, 1884. Its motto covers the farm, the orchard, and the fireside. Two dollars a year bought news, advice, and letters from working farmers across the Midwest.

One writer tells how he raised his corn yield past ninety bushels an acre by small experiments. Other pages carry market reports, household hints, and questions answered in print. Such weeklies were the internet of their day for country readers. A single surviving issue shows what prairie families worried about, planted, and hoped for in midwinter 1884.
2285-ridgway-of-montana-a-story-of-to-da:
William MacLeod Raine's western hero Ridgway comes to Montana as a modern man in a raw land, facing cattle barons, gunmen, and a woman whose trust he must earn. Ridgway of Montana mixes range warfare with romance, as its hero uses brains as well as a gun to survive. The title's boast about its hero signals Raine's confident, pulpy style.

The novel moves fast through stampedes, ambushes, and courtroom showdowns. Raine knew the West's stories from the inside and wrote dozens of such tales. Fans of classic westerns will find this one energetic and unpretentious.
22897-the-ideal:
Two talkers argue about time in The Ideal, a dialogue in an old-fashioned vein. The Friar looks up and echoes his companion. Time is, indeed, he says. Uttering the word time, the Friar argues, must mean asserting something beyond its bare existence. That existence itself he treats as beyond doubt, since without time nothing could be at all.

From that playful knot the talk ranges over what an ideal is and whether it can exist outside minds. The piece belongs to a tradition of philosophical dialogue written for general readers, more fencing match than lecture. Its pleasure lies in watching an abstract word get chased around a room. Readers who enjoy talk-driven pieces will find a curious, mannered performance preserved here.
23157-other-people-s-business-the-romant:
Harriet Lummis Smith inspects a chair in Other People's Business, the romantic career of the practical Miss Dale, published in 1916. Persis has just rescued her furniture, tactfully, from a heavy guest. Her appraising glance at the vacated chair confirms the damage. Front rung sprung, exactly as expected, and Etta West ought to know better.

Persis Dale's practicality is her fortune and her comedy. She runs a boarding world of other people's business while her own romance assembles itself under her nose. Smith keeps the observation at chair-rung level, where character actually shows. The novel offers small-town American comedy of the sunniest kind, with a heroine whose competence the plot must teach her to set down, briefly, for love.
2438-daphne-an-autumn-pastoral:
Margaret Sherwood's Daphne: An Autumn Pastoral is a romance of the Italian countryside, where an American woman and an Italian shepherd find love among olive groves and ruins. The novella takes its mood from the season: golden light, ripe harvests, and a sense of time passing. Sherwood writes the landscape with a poet's care.

The story's charm lies in its atmosphere rather than its plot, and its gentle romance suits quiet reading. Readers who love Italy in fiction will enjoy its warmth. It is a small, lovely book. Sherwood taught at Wellesley and wrote several Italian romances.
3652-history-of-the-mackenzies-with-gene:
Alexander Mackenzie writes a history of the Mackenzies, a great Highland clan, with genealogies of its principal families. The book traces the clan from its early chiefs through centuries of war, landholding, and loyalty in Ross-shire and beyond. Mackenzie, a historian of the Highlands, gathers charters, traditions, and family trees into one record.

Readers meet chiefs, cadet branches, and the septs that served them, with the feuds and marriages that shaped the north. The genealogies make the volume useful for descendants tracing Mackenzie lines. The book suits readers interested in Scottish clan history and in the Highlands before and after the Jacobite risings.
3709-love-eternal:
H Rider Haggard builds this novel around two souls who meet as children and keep finding each other through a lifetime of partings. Isobel and Godfrey grow up side by side, sharing a garden and a chapel. Then years apart pull them in opposite ways, with India, France, and the church claiming Godfrey while marriage and duty claim Isobel. Haggard frames their bond as a love that outlasts single lives, with dreams, spirit rappings, and ghostly hands testing what the pair believe.

The later chapters turn earnest, as Godfrey takes orders and the lovers weigh faith against feeling. Readers who know Haggard for adventure tales will find a slower, more inward book here, though ghosts and foreign scenes still crowd the pages. It is a romance about constancy, and it asks whether love can hold its shape across time, distance, and death itself.
3735-the-inspector-general:
Nikolay Gogol wrote this five act comedy about a small Russian town that mistakes a penniless young traveler for a government inspector sent in secret from Saint Petersburg. The mayor and his officials, each with his own petty corruption to hide, rush to bribe and flatter the supposed great man, who accepts their money with cheerful ease. Dobchinsky's gossip, Anna's questions about the stranger's age, and the tour of charitable institutions all feed the panic.

The play is a national classic in Russia, where its name alone calls up a whole world of bribery and fear. Thomas Seltzer's translation keeps the talk brisk and the jokes pointed. Readers who like satire will enjoy watching a town condemn itself out of its own mouth, while the true inspector is still on the road.
4031-the-london-prodigal:
A comedy of London life follows a young prodigal whose waste and swagger trouble his family and tempt his friends. In the sampled scenes, a Devonshire lad boasts of his purse and person, while Lucy whispers aside that it is Arthur she loves, not the rich suitor pressed on her.

Lovers, fathers, and sharp-tongued servants trade verse and prose in the manner of the early English stage. The play mixes farce, romance, and moral warning, as the prodigal learns the cost of his pleasures. Readers who enjoy Shakespeare-era comedy will find a lively, old-fashioned piece about money, love, and coming home.
4046-the-garden-of-survival:
Algernon Blackwood's novel opens with a letter about talent raised beyond its own height by a guiding hand. The writer and his sibling, puzzled and happy, ask whose unerring hand shaped the result, and promise another curious item in the tale to come.

The garden of the title stands for a place where art, love, and a strange power meet. Blackwood writes in his usual mode of quiet wonder, where the unseen presses close on daily life. Readers who enjoy supernatural fiction without shock will find a gentle, thoughtful story of growth and mystery.
411-the-king-s-jackal:
Richard Harding Davis sets this Tangier tale among exiled kings, guards, and plotters on a hotel terrace. The King of Messina, in hiding under a false name, waits for a boat from Gibraltar while his majordomo scans the sea. Soldiers of the Sultan guard his door, and a colonel frets over each delay.

Davis writes bright, swift scenes of Mediterranean color, court intrigue, and comic suspense. The jackal of the title serves a greater beast, a schemer who feeds on royal hopes. The book reads as a light adventure of old Morocco, full of sun, sea, and whispered plots.
4206-the-letters-of-franklin-k-lane-pers:
The letters of Franklin K. Lane, personal and political, show a public man writing to friends, officials, and reformers. One letter praises self-respecting Gaelic-speaking Scots from the northern islands, crofters driven from Highland homes to make place for sheep and fine estates.

Another calls the express job the biggest one yet, claiming a real service to country and express companies alike, which must improve service and rates or face government action. The collection suits readers who like American progressivism in its own voice, frank and practical. Crofters, express rates, and government power share his letters.
4963-moral:
Ludwig Thoma's play Moral arrives with an introductory sketch of the author's career, from law practice abandoned in 1899 to humorous verse for Simplicissimus under the pen name Pete Schlemiehl. His poems, later collected as Grobheiten, nearly identified the paper with his name, and his Bavarian dialect prose and boyhood tales won a large audience.

Thoma became editor of Simplicissimus in 1899, and his renown grew from there, with critics ranking him next to Hauptmann in modern German drama. When Moral appeared, reviewers called its author shocking yet casting a long shadow. Readers get a German satirist at his sharpest, introduced by the career that made his mockery matter.
5128-the-young-carthaginian-a-story-of-t:
G. A. Henty's adventure novel for young readers follows a Carthaginian hero through the age of Hannibal. From a camp in the desert and the streets of Carthage, the story moves to a campaign in Spain, the siege of Saguntum, the crossing of the Rhone. The great battles of the Trebia and Lake Trasimene follow.

Henty wrote for boys who, as his preface notes, often sympathised with Carthage against Rome, and he fills the book with battles, plots, and escapes. The novel doubles as a lively introduction to the Punic Wars, told from the losing side, with history carried along by a hero who is always in the thick of it.
533-the-song-of-the-cardinal:
Gene Stratton-Porter follows a cardinal bird through a year of song, storm, and love in this nature novel. The cardinal, a yearling of bright crest and black beard, hatches in the Limberlost marsh, then wings south to orange orchards. Five chapters take their names from his cries: good cheer, wet year, come here, so dear, see here.

Stratton-Porter writes the bird's life with close, loving detail, from slugs at breakfast to mates and nests. Men hear his song as a message of cheer. The book charms as a nature romance where a small bird's year mirrors human hope, grief, and joy.
575-the-essays-or-counsels-civil-and-mor:
Francis Bacon gathers his famous essays on life, rule, and conduct in this volume, dedicated to the Duke of Buckingham. Topics run from truth, death, and revenge to love, envy, travel, friendship, riches, and studies. Bacon enlarged the essays in number and weight, calling them a new work.

His style is terse, sententious, and full of maxims meant for men of business and courts. Each essay weighs a subject from several sides in a few pages. The book endures as a founding text of the English essay, where wisdom arrives in short, sharp sentences.
5883-the-flying-saucers-are-real:
Donald Keyhoe investigates flying saucers in The Flying Saucers Are Real, dedicating the book to Helen with love. Keyhoe, who relates his investigation in these pages, writes with the urgency of a reporter convinced the subject deserves serious attention. Twenty chapters follow sightings, official statements, and the arguments for and against unexplained craft in American skies.

The volume offers a landmark of early UFO literature, written before saucers became pop culture shorthand. Keyhoe gathers cases, questions secrecy, and presses for open inquiry, in plain, earnest prose. The book suits readers of UFO history, Cold War culture, and popular science debates, offering the founding argument that something real flies unexplained overhead.
590-robert-louis-stevenson-a-record-an-e:
Alexander Japp gathers memories, letters, and criticism of Robert Louis Stevenson in this 1905 tribute. Chapters treat Treasure Island, travels, the Vailima letters, and Stevenson's genius, methods, and gloom, with facsimile letters and a Samoan memorial. Friends such as Henley, Gosse, and Stedman add estimates, some fond, some sharp.

Japp writes as a friend who read Stevenson's proofs in Davos while author and wife lay ill. His record stresses Stevenson's cheer, craft, and moral seriousness. The book serves as a rich early life-and-letters volume, where those who knew Stevenson best speak in their own words.
6070-the-unwilling-vestal:
Edward Lucas White tells a tale of Rome under the Caesars. As the jacket claims, it gives for the first time in fiction a correct account of the Vestal Virgins, their powers and privileges, and many strange Roman customs and beliefs. First published in 1918, the book went through sixteen printings.

White pairs a rattling good story with full knowledge of Roman life, bringing to imperial Rome the picturesqueness that marked his South American novel El Supremo. The unwilling vestal at the center must serve a sacred office she did not choose. The result is a vivid pageant of priests, power, and private will.
6404-more-pages-from-a-journal:
Mark Rutherford, in a 1910 Oxford volume, offers more pages from a journal with other papers, dedicated to Horace and Susan E. P. Smith as an inadequate acknowledgement of a great debt. A bad dream, Esther, Kate Radcliffe, and Mr. Whittaker's retirement open the contents, with confessions of a self tormentor, letters to the Rambler and from the authoress of Judith Crowhurst, and a clearing up after a January storm.

The end of the north wind, Romney Marsh, Axmouth, and the preacher and the sea follow. Conversion, July, a Sunday morning in November, Beachy Head in December, dreaming, ourselves, and the riddle come next. A later paper tells of a manager who was the pivot of his firm, until illness and a wife's death let junior partners divide his work. Rutherford writes quiet, inward prose, where a dream or a marsh walk carries a life's moral weight.
6452-right-royal:
John Masefield's Right Royal is a poem whose persons, horses, and events are imaginary, with no reference to any living person or horse. An hour before the race, lovers Charles Cothill and the golden lady Em talk in mild March weather. He is from Sleins, a manor up the Lithe, made stalwart, springy, and swift by riding the Downs, with dark honest eyes, a fine firm mouth, and wind tan on his skin.

He is to ride Right Royal, his own horse, in the English Chaser's Cup on Compton Course, colours under a pale coat reaching to his spurs. A mid passage shows Em cheering him, proud to see him followed by all the crowd, picking Right Royal, Soyland, and Peterkin first, second, and third. Masefield writes racing as romance, where a horse, a rider, and a lover's faith carry a whole spring afternoon.
6597-perpetual-light-a-memorial:
William Rose Benét writes a memorial in verse for a woman now gone, whose face, he says, is no longer of this world. The epigraph speaks of a man without wings who rejoiced in a companion God gave him, and who heard her sigh with her head on his shoulder. Grief here is bitter as myrrh, yet lit by faith in a festival of perpetual light.

Dedicated to Kathleen and Margaret, the poems ask readers to think not of verse, but of her alone, and of the light she left on stone. Benét keeps the language tender and high, with day and night made bright by her memory. Perpetual Light is a short, moving book of mourning, where love outlasts loss.
6817-chaitanya-and-the-vaishnava-poets-o:
John Beames studies Chaitanya and the Vaishnava poets of Bengal in a paper from the Indian Antiquary of 1873, on Bengali poetry of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The Padkalpataru, or wish-granting tree of song, may be taken as the scriptures of the Vaishnava sect in Bengal, he explains. It is a collection of songs by many poets in many ages. They are arranged to show the sect's views in full.

Put together in recent times, the collection spans devotion, love, and theology in lyric form. Beames writes as a scholar of language and faith. Chaitanya and the Vaishnava Poets of Bengal is a learned, early guide to a rich devotional poetry.
7066-under-the-prophet-in-utah-the-natio:
Frank Cannon, formerly United States senator from Utah, with Harvey O'Higgins, warns of a political priestcraft in Under the Prophet in Utah. Contents run from the days of the raid and a mission to Washington, through without a country, the manifesto, and the road to freedom, to the goal and after. First betrayals, the church and the interests, and the crossways lead to the downward path and the will of the Lord.

The conspiracy completed, the Smoot exposure, treason triumphant, and the struggle for liberty follow, with the price of protest, the new polygamy, and the prophet of Mammon. A note recalls O'Higgins meeting Cannon in Denver in spring 1910, while working with Judge Lindsey on The Beast and the Jungle. The book is a Progressive era charge against church rule in politics.
7296-john-m-synge-a-few-personal-recolle:
John Masefield recalls John M. Synge from a first meeting in Bloomsbury on a Monday night in January 1903, in a friend's room up two pairs of stairs. Synge sat in a rush-bottomed chair talking to a young man down from Oxford. Then he stood to shake hands, a man of middle height, about five feet eight or nine, with a dark, grave face full of changing liveliness.

Masefield's recollections, with biographical notes, follow that first impression into friendship and work, sketching a playwright whose quiet manner hid a sharp eye. The memoir gives Synge in talk and habit rather than in formal biography, warm and observant. Readers meet the man behind the plays, as a friend saw him.
750-the-high-history-of-the-holy-graal:
An unknown author wrote this Old French romance in the early thirteenth century as a continuation of Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished Perceval. Sebastian Evans made the English translation in 1898. The tale follows knights of Arthur's court in quest of the Holy Graal, the vessel of the Last Supper, through forests, castles, and hermitages.

The knights face tests of faith, chastity, and courage, and the story blends chivalry with deep Christian allegory. Perceval, Galahad, and their fellows seek a vision that only the pure may grasp. The book is a cornerstone of Grail legend, and it shaped how later ages imagined the quest for a holy thing.
7522-king-coal:
Upton Sinclair's novel takes its title from the power that rules the Colorado coal country. Its four books name the kingdom in order: The Domain of King Coal, The Serfs of King Coal, The Henchmen of King Coal, and The Will of King Coal. Sinclair, who had consecrated his life to agitation for social justice, enrolled his art in that cause, never flinching from sacrifice for it.

The story follows a young man who goes to work in the mines and learns the company town from inside: its dangers, its debts, its spies, and its hunger for liberty. Sinclair does not rest with description; he appeals to the honor and good fellowship of his readers, opening their eyes to conditions under which wage earners lived. King Coal is a novel of protest, written to move as well as to show.
7973-napoleon-s-campaign-in-russia-anno-:
Dr A. Rose wrote this medico-historical study of Napoleon's Russian campaign of 1812, following the Grand Army from its crossing of the Niemen in June to the retreat through Wiasma, Smolensk, and the Beresina. His chapters cover Moscow under occupation, the governor Rostopchine, prisoners of war, and the treatment of typhus after the second crossing of the Niemen. The preface notes that of some six hundred thousand men who crossed, most never came home.

Rose's focus is medical as much as military: cold, hunger, and disease killed more soldiers than battles did. He draws on regimental lists and archives to show how an army dissolved. For readers of military history, the book adds the surgeon's view to the familiar story of 1812, and explains why the retreat became a byword for disaster.
7977-purgatory-doctrinal-historical-and-:
Mrs J. Sadlier wrote this Catholic book on purgatory in three modes at once: doctrine, history, and poetry. Dedicated to her son, the Reverend Francis X. Sadlier, who died in November 1885 scarcely three months after ordination, it gathers teaching on the souls in purgatory with legends, historic lore, and verse. Its epigraph comes from Psalm 141, praying that God bring the soul out of prison.

Sadlier, who had written and translated many Catholic books, aimed to comfort the bereaved and encourage prayer for the dead. The mixture of argument, story, and poetry makes the doctrine feel lived rather than abstract. As a piece of nineteenth-century Catholic devotion, it shows how ordinary believers were taught to think about death, mercy, and the communion of the living and the dead.
7983-the-vitamine-manual:
Walter H. Eddy, associate professor of physiological chemistry at Teachers College, Columbia University, wrote this manual on the new food factors then called vitamines. Its chapters cover how vitamines were discovered, attempts to work out their chemical nature, methods of testing, the yeast test for vitamine B. Their sources, properties, use in diets, and the diseases caused by their lack, with a bibliography. Eddy aimed the book at both students and lay readers.

The manual is frank that its science was moving fast and that some data would soon be out of date. Its lasting interest is historical: it captures nutrition at the moment vitamins were newly understood and already changing diets. Students of medicine and food history will find a clear, compact record of that turning point.
8116-the-communistic-societies-of-the-un:
Charles Nordhoff visited and observed the communistic societies of the United States and reported them from personal experience. His book opens with an inquiry into labour, the condition and necessities of workers, and the mistakes of the trades-unions, then turns to the societies themselves. Amana in 1874, with its history, social habits, and religion; the Harmonists at Economy, with Father Rapp and their creed; and the Separatists at Zoar, among others.

Nordhoff writes as a sympathetic journalist, describing daily life, worship, and work in communities that tried to live by sharing. His accounts remain the best contemporary record of American utopian experiments. For readers of social history, the book is an engaging tour of a radical America that sought a better way to live together.
8199-the-moon-metal:
Garrett P. Serviss wrote this science-fiction novella around a discovery of gold at the south pole, news that nobody suspected would begin a new era in the world's history. Its chapters follow the magician of science, Dr Syx, the Grand Teton mine, the wealth of the world, wonders of the new metal, a strange discovery. A detective of science, the top of the Grand Teton, the fate of a kite, and finally the looting of the moon and the last of Dr Syx.

Serviss imagines a metal from the moon that upends the world's money, since gold itself loses its scarcity. The tale mixes adventure with economics, as nations and markets reel from the new wealth. For science-fiction readers, it is an early and inventive example of the genre, and a sharp fable about value itself.
824-speeches-literary-and-social:
Charles Dickens gathered his public speeches on literary and social topics in this volume, issued in 1880. He spoke at dinners, institutes, and charities, praising books, libraries, and the workers who spread learning. Added chapters study Dickens as a letter writer, poet, and public reader of his own works.

The speeches show Dickens the citizen, warm, witty, and earnest about reform. He urges kindness to the poor, support for schools, and honour for the craft of writing. The book gives readers the novelist in his own voice off the page, and it is a rich source for his views on the age he described.
8998-paris-as-it-was-and-as-it-is-a-sket:
An English traveler wrote this sketch of Paris in a series of letters home during 1801 and 1802, printed in London in 1803. The writer compares Paris before the Revolution with Paris after it, asking what changed in science, letters, arts, religion, schools, manners, and amusements. Public buildings and national institutions get close notice.

The letters were penned in the brief peace between Britain and France, and a planned map of Paris never reached the book, held at Calais when war broke out anew. That mishap only adds to the book's charm. It stands as a sharp, on-the-spot report of a capital remade by revolt.
9253-browne-s-folly-from-the-doliver-rom:
Writing from the Wayside in August 1860, Hawthorne answers a cousin who asked for a story for the Essex Institute. He confesses he can write no story now, years after Twice-Told Tales and Mosses from an Old Manse. His mind, he says, has lost the plan and measure of those little narratives, once so fertile.

Instead he describes a conspicuous hill near Salem, where he once meant to set a dreamy fiction. He knows not if it lies in Salem, Danvers, or Beverly. The letter is a charming apology, and a glimpse of a tale Hawthorne never wrote, haunting the hill still.
9303-post-augustan-poetry-from-seneca-to:
H. E. Butler, a fellow of New College, Oxford, wrote this history of Roman poetry after Augustus, from Seneca to Juvenal. The opening chapter treats decline: the principate, emperors from Tiberius to Nero, and the decay of Roman character. Great Augustan poets, Butler says, barred further advance, and schools taught rhetoric over true learning.

Later chapters cover drama, Seneca, and the poets who followed, with notes on stage, mime, and recitation. Butler judges each age with care. The book remains a clear guide to a period of Latin verse too often skipped, learned yet readable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-bern:
Agostino Bernal, Spanish theologian of Magallon in Aragon, was born in 1587. He died at Saragossa on 13 September 1642. He joined the Jesuits in 1603, aged sixteen. Classically finished, he taught humanities and rhetoric with success. Most of his life, however, went to professing philosophy and theology at Saragossa, ending there.

A man of rare innocence and candour of soul, his love of prayer was so great it would be hard to say whether meditation or study took more of his time. Many looked on him as one of his age's most learned men. His published works are Disputationes de Divini Verbi Incarnatione, Saragossa 1639, and Disputationes de Sacramentis in genere, Eucharistia et Ordine, Lyons 1651, a posthumous work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-vandal:
Albert Vandal was a French writer born at Paris in July 1853 and dead there in August 1910. His father directed the postal service under the Second Empire. Vandal joined the Council of State as auditor, but family tradition and moderate, liberal views cost him his post under the Republic. He became the disciple and friend of Albert Sorel, professor of diplomatic history, and later succeeded him in the chair.

Vandal's first book, a travel account of Sweden and Norway, appeared in 1876. It was followed by works on Louis XV and Elizabeth of Russia and on the French embassy in the East. The book that fixed his reputation was Napoleon and Alexander I, which twice won the Gobert grand prize and opened the French Academy to him in 1897. He later published on the advent of Bonaparte and joined fellow Catholics in writing to the pope after the law separating Church and State.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-frontal:
The altar frontal, or antipendium, covers the altar front, from table to predella and gospel corner to epistle side. It grew from silk or precious curtains veiling the space under the altar, later joined into one drapery hung from the table. A partial frontal is forbidden, and an altar facing the people at the back needs its back covered too.

No material is prescribed. Precious metals with enamels and jewels, painted or gilt wood, cloth of gold, velvet, or silk usually match the vestments. It may bear Christ's image, scenes from his life, or emblems such as lamb, pelican, chalice and host. The altar's patron saint may appear too, but never skulls or cross-bones on a black frontal. Where the altar front is beautifully painted or a reliquary stands beneath a column-borne table, the frontal may be unnecessary, though solemn occasions call for richer ones.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-marec:
Ambrose Maréchal, third Archbishop of Baltimore, was born at Ingres near Orléans in 1764 and died at Baltimore in 1828. Set for law by his parents, he entered Orléans's Sulpician seminary, took tonsure late in 1787, and, fleeing revolutionary chaos, was ordained at Bordeaux in 1792. On ordination day, at life's risk with Abbés Richard, Martignon, and Cicquard, he sailed for America, reaching Baltimore on 24 June 1792 for his first Mass.

He served missions in St. Mary's County and Bohemia, taught theology at St. Mary's in 1799 and Georgetown's staff in 1801. He then taught in France at Saint-Flour, Lyons, Aix, and Marseilles under Napoleon. Back in Baltimore in 1812, he declined Philadelphia in 1816 and became coadjutor to Archbishop Neale in 1817. He was consecrated Archbishop of Baltimore in December 1817 after Neale's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belial:
Belial is a short doctrinal and scriptural entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, untangling a name many readers take for a devil. It explains that in Hebrew the word is not a proper name at all, but a phrase for worthlessness or wickedness. Only in later translation did it harden into a personal name for evil.

The entry walks through Bible passages where translators render the same Hebrew word in different ways, sometimes as Belial and sometimes as the devil. It notes the famous contrast in Paul's second letter to Corinth, where Belial stands for darkness against Christ as light. Milton's separate demon of impurity gets a brief correcting note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedictional:
The Benedictional, a book of blessings used in the Church, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Its Latin name, Benedictionale, marks it as a collection of benedictions, or formal blessings, drawn largely from ancient sacramentaries, books of prayers for Mass. Some manuscripts scatter the blessings through the book, while others gather them apart.

A famous manuscript in the imperial library at Vienna gave the collection its name when Lambecius edited it, believing his edition the first. The entry corrects him, noting that nearly all its blessings had already appeared in print elsewhere. It is a brief note on a book's name and tangled publishing history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-lo:
Bernardino López de Carvajal, a Spanish cardinal, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Plasencia in 1455, he died at Rome in 1523. Nephew of the famed Cardinal Juan Carvajal, he rose fast at Rome under Sixtus IV, holding Astorga, then Badajoz, then Cartagena, three Spanish sees in turn.

As nuncio to Spain and then Spanish ambassador to Alexander VI, he moved between courts with ease, and Alexander made him cardinal in 1493. Later years brought the troubled Council of Pisa and a fall from favour, followed by restoration. The entry sketches a courtier-prelate of the Renaissance papacy at its most worldly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-betrothal:
Betrothal, the promise of future marriage, receives a full canon-law entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its Latin name is sponsalia, and the Church defines it as a deliberate, free, mutual promise, put into words, between two fit persons. It is a true compact, not a mere intention, and it needs care matching the weight of what it promises.

A one-sided promise, even if accepted, does not make a betrothal, and force, grave fear, or substantial error can void it. A valid betrothal binds the parties in justice to marry, and creates an impediment of public decency toward relatives. The entry maps a promise that law once treated almost like marriage itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-joanna-of-: Blessed Joanna of Portugal, daughter of King Alfonso V, was born at Lisbon in 1452 and died at Aveiro in 1490. From childhood she resolved to be Christ's spouse and enter religion. She resisted with courage every attempt by father and brother to marry her off. As heir in default of male issue, her refusal angered family and country. Princes sought her hand in vain, and she once ruled as regent in her father's absence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blaise-pascal:
Blaise Pascal, the French mathematician, physicist, and religious writer, is the subject of this long 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Clermont-Ferrand in 1623, he died in Paris in 1662. His father taught him grammar, Latin, Spanish, and mathematics by an original method, and at twelve he wrote on sounds, at sixteen on conic sections.

At Rouen he built an arithmetical machine to ease his father's tax calculations. A night of religious conversion, recorded in a paper sewn into his coat, turned him to Port-Royal and Jansenism. His Provincial Letters of 1656 defended the Jansenists with wit, and his Pensées, left unfinished, remain a classic of Christian apology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-pro:
Canonical provision is the regular way a vacant benefice, a church office with income, is filled. The entry breaks it into three steps: choosing the person, granting the title through canonical institution, and installing the holder in possession. People may be chosen by election, presentation, recommendation, resignation in someone's favor, or an approved exchange. A proper superior must still confirm the choice.

Greater offices usually come from the pope and lesser ones from the bishop. The bishop normally fills every office in his own diocese, though the pope's full jurisdiction lets him appoint anywhere. The entry recalls English statutes of 1351 and 1390 that resisted papal appointments. Such extraordinary provisions now occur only in defined cases. Appointment letters, it adds, are normally required.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal:
A cardinal is a dignitary of the Roman Church and counselor of the pope. The word once meant any priest permanently attached to a church. It comes from the Latin cardo, or hinge, and later meant a principal or excellent priest of a central church. The entry follows the office through its origin, growth, and changes across ten sections, from cardinal priests, deacons, and bishops to titles, dioceses, and deaconries.

Later sections weigh the cardinals' ties to bishops and to the pope, their nomination, duties, and rights, and the life of the College of Cardinals itself. Examples range from prominent priests at Constantinople, Milan, Ravenna, and Cologne to the great medieval holders of the office. The result is a full institutional history of a rank that grew from parish attachment into the body that counsels the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathedral:
A cathedral is the chief church of a diocese, where the bishop has his throne and nearby his residence. In the strict sense it is the bishop's own church, where he presides, teaches, and leads worship for the whole community. The name comes from the Greek and Latin for throne, and in early church writing it always carried the idea of authority.

The article recalls Christ's words about the scribes seated on the chair of Moses. It also recalls the feasts honoring Peter's chair at Antioch and Rome, showing how the throne became the chief symbol of authority. It distinguishes the cathedral from a merely episcopal church. It also sets it apart from the churches of archbishops, metropolitans, primates, and patriarchs, and notes that the East simply calls the bishop's church the great church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceremonial:
A ceremonial is the book that gives the full order for religious ceremony and solemn worship in ecclesiastical functions. At present only two official liturgical books bear the title: the Caeremoniale Romanum and the Caeremoniale Episcoporum. The Missal, Breviary, Ritual, and Pontifical also contain directions for Mass, the Office, the sacraments, and episcopal functions. So in a certain sense they may be counted ceremonials.

But their main purpose is to give the texts of the liturgical prayers. Directions are added only in general terms, so they are not regarded as ceremonials in the accepted sense. The oldest ceremonial books and rituals of the Roman Church go by the name Ordines Romani. Mabillon enumerates fifteen of them. They treat the choice of a Roman pontiff, Mass, Baptism and Holy Orders, and functions for special days of the year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-bur:
A long entry on Christian burial, the interment of the dead with church rites in consecrated ground. Jews and most ancient peoples buried their dead, while Greeks and Romans used both burial and cremation. Early Christians used burial only, as Tertullian attests, resting on the resurrection of the body and its likeness to Christ's rising, and on Jewish custom in Tobit, Sirach, and Maccabees.

Canon law lets every person choose his burial ground, even without a formal will, on any reasonable proof, including a confessor's word. The entry sets out the Church's law and rites and its recent prohibitions of cremation. It links cremation to materialism and opposition to Catholic teaching rather than hygiene. It also covers the Greek Church's burial rite, with notes on absolution crosses and burial law authorities such as Lex and Sagmüller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ciudad-real:
Ciudad Real is a bishopric-priorate of Spain's Military Orders, directly subject to the Holy See. The military orders of Santiago, Alcantara, Calatrava, and Montesa held scattered church lands. Article Six of the Concordat of 1851 ordered a single circumscription, a coto redondo, for them, governed by a prior of episcopal rank.

Pius the Ninth created the bishopric-priorate in 1875 by the bull Ad Apostolicam Beati Petri, giving it the whole province of Ciudad Real, drawn from Toledo, Cuenca, and Cordova. The bishop resides at Ciudad Real, population 15,327 in 1900. Alfonso the Twelfth and his successors, as Grand Masters of the orders, nominate the bishop-prior within three months of a vacancy. He takes the titular title of Bishop of Dora. The Cardinal Archbishop of Toledo executed the bull on 4 June 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Sister St. Euphrosine's entry follows the Congregation of Notre Dame de Montreal through foundress Marguerite Bourgeoys, born at Troyes on 17 April 1620. Third child of merchant Abraham Bourgeois, she answered Paul de Maisonneuve's 1653 invitation to teach at Ville Marie, Montreal. She sailed that June, giving herself to works of mercy. Her first school opened on 30 April 1657. A return to France won four companions, then a boarding school, an industrial school, and sodalities.

In 1670 she sailed again, returning in 1672 with royal letters and six new companions. In 1675 she built Notre Dame de Bon Secours chapel. Seeking freedom of action, she founded an unenclosed community under simple vows, winning Quebec's bishop's approbation and pressing those terms into rule. Sisters taught at Ville Marie and trained young women as Christian teachers. Later missions spread across Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, with day and boarding schools teaching all fundamental branches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corporal:
Herbert Thurston's entry treats the corporal, from Latin corpus, body. It is a square white linen cloth, now usually somewhat smaller than an altar's breadth, on which the Sacred Host and chalice rest during Mass. Though formal evidence is wanting, something in the corporal's nature may fairly be assumed in use since Christianity's earliest days. Early stages blur the corporal with the altar-cloth.

Saint Optatus, about 375, asks what Christian is unaware that in celebrating the Sacred Mysteries the altar's wood is covered with a linen cloth, leaving doubt which cloth he means. This likely forms the earliest direct testimony. Very probably the early centuries used only one large linen cloth, serving both as altar-cloth and corporal, doubled back to cover the gifts. Existing liturgical rules forbid embroidery on the corporal and require pure white linen throughout, though many exceptions seem to have existed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dungal:
Dungal, an Irish monk who taught, studied the stars, and wrote verse, flourished about 820. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry places him in 811 at Saint-Denis near Paris, an Irish priest and scholar. That year he wrote to Charlemagne explaining an eclipse of the sun thought to have occurred in 810. Alcuin calls him a bishop in one letter, and in 823 a capitulary of Lothair names him. In 825 an imperial decree made him master of the school at Pavia.

That is the last imperial record of him, but in 827 or 828 he wrote against Claudius of Turin in defense of images. Since he left his books to Saint Columbanus at Bobbio, he likely spent his last days in that Irish monastery. The entry gathers a career pieced together from charters and letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-encyclical:
An encyclical is, by its Greek roots, a circular letter, and this entry explains how usage narrowed the word. In modern times it means almost only papal documents. They differ in form from Bulls and Briefs. Their heading addresses the patriarchs, primates, archbishops, and bishops of the universal Church in communion with Rome. By exception, some go to the bishops of one country alone.

Thus Pius X's letter of January 1907 to the bishops of France counts as an encyclical. It was issued in French rather than Latin. Leo XIII's Longinqua Oceani of 1895 to the bishops of the United States does not bear the name, though it keeps the form. Encyclicals to the whole Church usually treat the Church's welfare. They condemn an error, warn of dangers to faith or morals, urge constancy, or prescribe cures. The entry prints the opening and close, using Pascendi on Modernism as its specimen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faro-portugal:
Faro is a Portuguese diocese in the southern Algarve, suffragan of Evora. Its see began at Ossonoba in 306 and lapsed under long Moorish rule. Restored at Silves in 1188, it passed in turn through Braga, Seville, and Lisbon. The episcopal title moved to Faro on 30 March 1577.

Its old cathedral began as a Roman basilica, later altered and rebuilt by Moorish hands. The diocese then counted 66 parishes, 214 churches, 112 priests, and many chapels. Some 228,000 Catholics lived within its wide bounds at the time. The article traces the see through Moorish conquest, transfer, and later revival.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-cab:
Francisco Cabral, born in the castle of Govillou in the diocese of Guarda, Portugal, in 1529 and dead at Goa in 1609, was a Portuguese Jesuit missionary in Japan. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1554 and, after his studies, went to Japan. There he laboured strenuously to spread the Christian religion, winning the friendship of princes and kings, several of whom, with their subjects, were brought to the faith by his zealous work.

He held high posts in his order's government in the East. They were superior of Japan for twelve years, master of novices, rector of the College of San Pablo at Goa, and visitor to India, the inspector of Jesuit missions there. He died at eighty-one with a reputation for prudence and holiness. He was a figure of the first century of the Japan mission, before persecution closed that field to the missionaries who had built it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-de-b:
Francois de Bonal, born in 1734 at the castle of Bonal near Agen and dead at Munich in 1800, was Bishop of Clermont through the French Revolution. As a clerical deputy to the Estates-General of 1789 he stood out for moderation and firmness.

 From prison Louis XVI asked whether he should receive Easter communion. Bonal answered with sympathy yet advised abstaining, since the king had sanctioned decrees destructive of religion, above all the civil constitution of the clergy. Refusing the constitutional oath, he fled through Flanders and Holland, was captured and sentenced to deportation, escaped, and spent his last years in German cities, leaving a Spiritual Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-de-m:
Francois de Montmorency Laval, born at Montigny-sur-Avre on 30 April 1623 and dead at Quebec on 6 May 1708, was the first Bishop of Canada. Scion of an illustrious family whose motto claimed God aid the first Christian baron, he studied under the Jesuits at La Fleche and at Clermont College in Paris. He joined a fervent group directed by Father Bagot that became the seed of the Seminary of Foreign Missions, sister to the future seminary of Quebec. His two elder brothers died in battle, leaving him the family title and estate.

 As bishop at Quebec he built the Canadian Church in hardship. The entry ranks him among the most holy figures of his age for mortification, humility, lively faith, and boundless charity to the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-ludwig-:
Franz Ludwig von Erthal, born at Lohr on the Main on 16 September 1730 and died at Wurzburg on 16 February 1795. He was Prince-Bishop of Wurzburg and Bamberg whose rule was a boon for Church and State. After theology at Mainz, Wurzburg, and Rome and law at Vienna, he became president of Wurzburg's secular government in 1762. Sent to Vienna in 1768 for the investiture of Prince-Bishop Adam Friedrich von Seinsheim, Joseph II made him imperial privy councillor and inspector of the Imperial Chamber at Wetzlar. In 1776 he served as imperial commissioner at the Diet of Ratisbon.

He succeeded Adam Friedrich at Wurzburg on 18 March 1779 and at Bamberg the following 12 April. As temporal ruler he put people's welfare above personal considerations, spending private means on charitable institutions, founding a model hospital at Bamberg and greatly improving and partly rebuilding St. Julius Hospital at Wurzburg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-kar:
Friedrich Karl Joseph von Erthal, the last Elector and Archbishop of Mainz, began as a reformer and ended as a champion of Febronianism. Born at Mainz in 1719, he held cathedral posts, led the university, and served as envoy at Vienna before taking the electorate in July 1774. His first act as bishop was to dismiss his predecessor's free-thinking councilors.

Soon he reversed course, filling Mainz University with Protestants and free-thinkers and shutting monasteries to fund it. With three fellow archbishops he issued the Punctuation of Ems in 1786, cutting papal power to a bare honor. Wars undid him: Campo-Formio in 1797 took his lands west of the Rhine, and the Concordat of 1801 took his rule over them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-funchal:
Funchal, a diocese in the Madeira Islands, takes its name from fennel, the plant that gave the town its Latin name. Madeira, known to Rome as Purpuraria, was claimed for Portugal in 1419, and vines from Crete planted in 1445 made the island famous. Leo X raised Funchal to a see in 1514, and Clement VII briefly made it an archdiocese over Goa, Cape Verde, and other far-flung suffragans.

Set on Madeira's south coast, Funchal became the first stop for ships bound to the New World and a hub of wealth, trade, and missions. The Portuguese ringed it with four forts, though cliffs already guarded it well. By 1909 the city held about 20,000 people, and the diocese counted some 150,000 Catholics served by ninety-three priests in fifty parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspar-de-car:
Gaspar de Carvajal, a Dominican missionary born in Extremadura around 1500, sailed down the Amazon with Orellana and lived to tell it. He reached Peru in 1533 for Indian missions, then joined Gonzalo Pizarro's 1540 push toward Quixos and the Amazon. Hunger and hostile tribes wore the party down until Pizarro sent Orellana down the Napo for food, with Carvajal aboard.

At the Amazon's meeting with the Napo, Orellana abandoned his comrades to the river's course. Carvajal and Sánchez de Vargas protested the treachery and were set ashore, later found by Pizarro in the wild. Only eighty of four hundred reached Quito in 1542. Carvajal then worked Tucumán for years, ruled his province, and died at Lima in 1584.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gradual:
The Gradual, in English often called the Grail, is the oldest and most important of the four chants of the choir's part of the Proper of the Mass. From the Latin graduale, a step, it represents, with its supplement the Tract or Alleluia, the singing of psalms alternating with Bible readings. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces a custom as old as the readings themselves.

The psalms at this place are an inheritance from the synagogue service. Alternate readings and psalms filled much of the first half of the liturgy everywhere from the beginning. Originally whole psalms were sung, in responsorial form. One reader chanted the text while the people answered each clause with an acclamation. The practice of whole psalms lasted until the fifth century, and singing them was for a time a privilege of deacons at Rome, suppressed by Gregory I in 595.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-fra:
Paris mathematician Guillaume-François-Antoine de l'Hôpital, born in 1661, gave the new differential calculus its first clear textbook. Meant for the army, he served as a cavalry captain until extreme near-sightedness forced him out. He had already solved problems set by Pascal at fifteen and studied mathematics in his tent.

In 1692 he spent four months learning the calculus from Jean Bernoulli at his estate near Vendôme. He then published his Analyse des infiniment petits in 1696, a careful guide to curves that let many readers grasp methods only a handful had known. The rule for fractions whose top and bottom both tend to zero still bears his name. His wife is said to have shared his work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-antoine-:
Jean-Antoine Chaptal, count of Chanteloup, was a French chemist and statesman born in 1756 at Nogaret and dead in Paris in 1832. Trained in medicine at Montpellier, he took the new chemistry chair there in 1781 and built chemical works of wide repute. He stayed in France through the Revolution, refusing posts abroad.

Chaptal improved gunpowder making at the Grenelle saltpetre works in 1793 and later taught at the Paris Polytechnic. Under Napoleon he sat on the Council of State and served as minister of the interior, setting up trade exchanges, chambers of commerce, and loan offices. He also brought the Sisters of Charity into hospital work and ordered the mineral water trade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-brehal:
Jean Bréhal, a French Dominican theologian who died about 1479, earned his place by clearing Joan of Arc's name. Doctor of theology at Caen in 1443, prior of Saint-Jacques in Paris, and inquisitor-general of France from 1452 to 1474, he stood high in church and university life.

At Charles VII's instance Bréhal reviewed the acts of Joan's trial, and on 7 July 1456 solemnly declared her condemnation unjust and wicked. His full inquiry, later printed by Dominican and Jesuit scholars, remains the backbone of her rehabilitation. He resigned in 1474 and spent his last years at Évreux in study and strict observance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-de-la-ca:
José de la Canal was a Spanish Augustinian friar and church historian who lived from 1768 to 1845. Born poor in Ucieda, in Santander province, he studied in Burgos convents, joined the Augustinian order in 1785, and later taught philosophy and kept the university library at Salamanca. A spell of confinement near Avila followed his liberal newspaper writing after King Ferdinand VII returned to Spain.

Canal is best known for carrying on España Sagrada, the great source collection on Spanish church history begun in 1743. Working with Antolín Merino and then alone, he produced volumes on the churches and monasteries of Gerona, drawing on archives he searched in Barcelona and Gerona. Readers turn to this entry for a clear account of a scholar who dug up unpublished records and checked them with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-mercado-:
José Mercado Rizal was a Filipino doctor, poet, and novelist who became his country's national hero. Born at Calamba in 1861, he studied in Manila and Spain, trained in eye medicine, and published the novel Noli me tangere in Berlin in 1886. The book satirized both friar landlords and Filipino society, and its sequel, El Filibusterismo, appeared in 1891.

Spanish officials linked his writing to rebellion, exiled him to Dapitan in Mindanao, and later tried and shot him in Manila on 30 December 1896.
